historical_timeline.summary: Fever and chills, possibly malaria or typhoid.
Throat pain and painful swallowing began at Long Branch, New Jersey.
Referred to the throat specialist Dr. John H. Douglas, who called the disease serious and epithelial in character.
Biopsy confirmed cancer of the right tonsillar pillar; judged beyond surgery.
Dictating his memoirs, written to offset the loss of his fortune to a Wall Street swindle, as speaking became painful.
Moved to a cottage on Mount McGregor, New York.
Died of throat cancer at Mount McGregor, days after finishing his memoirs.

claims.statement: Hiram Ulysses Grant was born on April 27, 1822, in Point Pleasant, Ohio, the first child of Jesse and Hannah Grant.
Grant died of throat cancer on July 23, 1885, at Mount McGregor, New York, days after completing his memoirs.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Record the death as a fact without graphic detail.

claims.statement: Grant was a heavy cigar smoker: his tobacco use rose during the Civil War to about eighteen to twenty cigars a day, and he reported smoking nine or ten a day in peacetime.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documents heavy cigar use; reported in a secondary medical-history essay.

claims.statement: In June 1884, at his summer home in Long Branch, New Jersey, Grant began to have stinging throat pain and pain on swallowing.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented onset that anchors the synthetic presentation.

claims.statement: On October 22, 1884, his physician Dr. Fordyce Barker referred Grant to the throat specialist Dr. John H. Douglas, who told him the disease was serious and epithelial in character.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Several months passed between the first symptoms and specialist evaluation.

source_links.locator: Biographical note: the fatal illness first manifested itself in the fall of 1884

claims.statement: Grant's physicians recorded a carcinoma of the right tonsillar pillar; a biopsy examined by Dr. George B. Elliot confirmed cancer at a consultation on February 19, 1885, and the doctors judged it beyond surgery.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented diagnosis that the synthetic modern diagnosis is linked to.

source_links.locator: Abstract: carcinoma of the right tonsillar pillar

claims.statement: Swallowing became so painful that Grant often went without food and water; his care was aimed at comfort, with cocaine applied to numb his throat and opiates taken reluctantly for pain, while he kept writing and, by May 1885, dictating his memoirs.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documents the symptom burden and the era's palliative options; described without graphic detail.

claims.statement: Grant's cancer has been attributed to his heavy cigar smoking; the specialist he consulted in 1884 suggested a link, and cigar smoking is now known to cause cancers of the mouth and throat.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A plausible causal attribution, not a documented finding; the synthetic tobacco problem is linked to it.

source_links.locator: Cigar smoking causes cancer of the oral cavity, larynx, esophagus, and lung

claims.statement: Grant had recurrent severe, incapacitating headaches, interpreted retrospectively as most likely migraines.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation; not placed on the active problem list.

claims.statement: In 1858 Grant had fever and chills, possibly from malaria or typhoid, and he had periodic fevers believed to have been malaria.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation of a historical fever; not placed on the active problem list.

claims.statement: Grant's father, Jesse Grant, died in 1873 at age 79; his mother, Hannah Grant, died in 1883.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The cited source does not give causes of death.

claims.statement: Late in life Grant lost his personal fortune to a Wall Street swindle and wrote his Civil War memoirs to offset the loss and provide for his wife.
In June 1885 Grant moved with his family to a cottage on Mount McGregor in Wilton, New York, chosen for its cool, dry air, where he died.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Sources differ by a day on the arrival date (June 16 or June 17, 1885).

source_links.locator: Left New York for Mount McGregor on June 17, 1885

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Recognize a persistent unilateral throat lesion with painful swallowing in a heavy tobacco user as possible head and neck cancer, refer urgently for laryngoscopy and biopsy with timely imaging, and provide primary-care supportive care around diagnosis: tobacco cessation, nutrition, dental preparation, symptom control, mood screening, and laboratory monitoring.

documentation.chief_complaint: Runny nose, cough, and low-grade fever for three days

hpi.narrative: Mr. Grant is a 62-year-old man who asked for a same-day visit. Last week the otolaryngologist biopsied an ulcerated lesion of his right tonsillar pillar, and pathology showed p16-negative squamous cell carcinoma. Staging PET/CT is booked for two days from now. He stopped cigars two weeks ago and takes varenicline 1 mg twice daily. Three days ago he developed a runny nose and sneezing, followed by a dry cough. His highest home temperature was 37.8 °C. Several people at a meeting he attended last week have had colds. Home COVID-19 antigen tests on the first and third days were negative. Coughing fits make his right-sided throat pain worse, now 6 of 10, up from 5 last week. He uses the lidocaine rinse before meals and the acetaminophen solution 20 mL up to four times a day. He has taken no other medicines, because he was unsure what was safe. He is still managing soft foods and two supplement drinks a day, and he has not choked or coughed while eating or drinking. His saliva was streaked with blood the day after the biopsy and has been clear since. The urge for a cigar is stronger when he coughs, but he has not smoked. He worries that the cough means the cancer has spread to his lungs.

ros.finding: Fatigue; temperature to 37.8 °C at home; no rigors or night sweats
Clear rhinorrhea and congestion; right-sided throat pain worse with coughing; no new bleeding from the biopsy site
Dry cough; no sputum, hemoptysis, wheeze, or breathlessness
No chest pain, palpitations, or ankle swelling
No vomiting or diarrhea; mild nausea only if varenicline is taken without food
Worried about the staging scan; sleep broken by cough; no low mood

exam.finding: Tired but well-appearing; speaking in full sentences; mildly hoarse
Tympanic membranes normal; nasal mucosa red and swollen with clear discharge
Ulcerated lesion of the right tonsillar pillar with a healing biopsy site; no active bleeding, pus, or new swelling
Firm right level II node, unchanged from the CT; no new or tender nodes
Unlabored; scattered upper-airway rhonchi that clear with coughing; no crackles, wheeze, or dullness
Drank 90 mL of water without coughing, throat clearing, or a wet voice

assessment_plan.display: Acute bronchitis, likely viral, after an upper respiratory infection
assessment_plan.assessment: Temperature 37.5 °C, heart rate 86, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 96 percent, and a clear chest make pneumonia unlikely. He passed the water swallow screen and has not choked with meals, so aspiration is also unlikely despite his dysphagia. A chest radiograph and antibiotics are not indicated
plan: Supportive care: honey in warm drinks, saline nasal rinse, and rest
Continue the acetaminophen solution at no more than 3,000 mg a day. Do not add combination cold or flu products, because most contain more acetaminophen
Avoid codeine-containing cough syrups. Plain dextromethorphan at night is acceptable if the cough disturbs sleep
Repeat a home COVID-19 antigen test in 48 hours. If it is positive, call the same day, because antiviral treatment would be offered at his age with cancer
The cough may last two to three weeks

assessment_plan.display: Squamous cell carcinoma of the right tonsillar pillar, staging in progress
assessment_plan.assessment: The cough fits a cold and is not a sign of spread to the lungs, which the staging scan will assess. A respiratory infection can cause inflammatory uptake in the chest and neck nodes on PET/CT
plan: Keep the staging PET/CT as booked. Message the head and neck team and radiology about the current cold so any reactive uptake is read in context
Treatment-planning visit next week as scheduled

assessment_plan.display: Nicotine dependence, cigars, two weeks abstinent
assessment_plan.assessment: Abstinent on varenicline. Cravings are stronger while he is ill and worried, a common relapse trigger. Coughing can increase for a few weeks after stopping smoking
plan: Continue varenicline 1 mg twice daily after meals
Brief counseling today: plan for cravings during illness and while waiting for results, and remove remaining cigars from the house
Offer the state quitline for extra support between visits

assessment_plan.display: Oropharyngeal dysphagia from the tonsillar tumor
assessment_plan.assessment: Swallowing is unchanged; weight 76.5 kg, down 0.5 kg in a week
plan: Continue soft, calorie-dense foods and two supplement drinks a day
Keep the 60-minute wait after the lidocaine rinse before eating or drinking, because a numbed throat raises the risk of choking
